title: The priest with a pot on his head
translation: Another story about a priest from Ninnaji. There was a farewell party for a boy who was about to become a priest, and everyone was having fun. One priest got drunk and carried away, grabbed a three-legged pot that stood nearby, and put it on his head. It was tight, but he squashed his nose flat, squeezed his face in, and came dancing out. The whole room loved it.
He danced for a while, then tried to pull it off. It would not come off. The party went quiet. What now?

Whatever they tried, the skin around his neck tore and bled, his head swelled up more and more, and he could hardly breathe. They tried to smash the pot, but it would not break easily, and the ringing inside was more than he could stand. So that was out too. In the end they threw a thin robe over the three legs, which stuck up like horns, led him by the hand with a walking stick, and took him to a doctor in the capital. People stared all the way.

You can imagine what he looked like, sitting face to face with the doctor. When he tried to speak, his voice just boomed around inside and nobody could understand a word. The doctor said there was nothing like this in the books and no treatment handed down either. So they took him back to Ninnaji, where his friends and his old mother sat by his pillow and wept. He probably could not even hear them.

Then someone said: "So he loses his ears and nose. He'll live, won't he? Just pull as hard as you can." They pushed straw in all around to keep the metal off his skin and pulled as if they meant to tear his head off. It came off, minus bits of ear and nose. He had barely escaped with his life, and he was ill for a long time afterwards.

literal: This too (is about) a Ninnaji priest: as a farewell for a boy who was about to become a priest, they were all enjoying themselves, and (one priest), drunk and carried away with the fun, took a three-legged pot that was nearby and put it on his head; it was tight, but he pressed his nose flat, pushed his face in and danced out, and the whole company was delighted beyond measure.
After dancing a while, he tried to pull it off, but it would not come off at all.
The banquet lost its fun, and they were at a loss, (thinking) 'what shall we do?'

Whatever they did, the skin around his neck broke and bled, it only swelled and swelled, and his breathing was blocked too, so they tried to break it, but it did not break easily, and it rang and was hard to bear, so they could not; having no way to deal with it, they threw a thin robe over the three-legged horns, led him by the hand, had him use a stick, and took him to a doctor in the capital; along the way, people stared in wonder without end.
The way he must have looked as he went in to the doctor and sat facing him: it must have been strange indeed.
When he spoke, it echoed in a muffled voice and could not be heard.

When (the doctor) said, 'Such a thing is not found in the books, and there is no teaching handed down', they went back to Ninnaji again; close friends, his old mother and others sat by his pillow and wept and grieved, but it did not seem that he could hear.

Meanwhile, someone said: 'Even if his ears and nose are torn off, why should his life at least not survive? Just put your strength in and pull'; so they pushed straw stalks in all around, kept the metal away (from the skin), and pulled as if to tear off his head, and with ears and nose torn and gouged, it came off.
He got away with a hard-won life and lay sick for a long time.

notes.quote: 童の法師にならむとする名残
notes.text: A boy who served at the temple ({童|わらは}) was about to take his vows and become a priest. The party says goodbye to his life as a boy.
A metal pot standing on three legs ({鼎|かなへ}). Upside down on a head, the three legs point up. The text itself calls them 'horns' ({角|つの}) later.

notes.quote: 満座興に入ること限りなし
notes.text: The first 'without limit' (限りなし): the room loves him. The second one comes in the street: 人の怪しみ見る事限りなし, people stare without limit. Same words, opposite situation.
{大|おほ}かた … ず: 'not at all'. The れ is the auxiliary る in its sense of 'can': 'could not be pulled off'.

notes.quote: 響きて堪へがたかりければ
notes.text: When you hit a metal pot on someone's head, it rings like a bell inside. So breaking it was out.
{帷子|かたびら}: a thin, unlined robe. They probably covered the pot to hide it. If so, it did not work.
けむ: a guess about the past, 'it must have been'. Kenkō was not there; he imagines the scene for you. With さこそ the ending takes the realis form, so けむ becomes けめ.
The doctor looks in the medical books ({書|ふみ}): no case on record, no standard treatment. Medicine by the book, around 1300.
らむ: a guess about the present, 'he probably hears'. They weep at his pillow, and he is inside a metal pot. The scene is dark, and it is very funny.
などか … む: 'why would he not…?', a rhetorical question that means 'of course he will'. The plan is: accept losing the ears and nose, and save the life.
からし: 'harsh, painful' (modern {辛|から}い 'spicy'). からき{命|いのち}: a life saved with great difficulty. Modern Japanese still says {辛|から}くも, 'narrowly'.
